summary: Provides example SIP test messages meant to stress, or torture, the code of IPv6-enabled SIP implementations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: These are tricky practice questions for phone software. If it handles them without getting confused, it is probably built well.

subtitle: Test cases for IPv6 support in SIP implementations.

tldr.problem: IPv6-enabled SIP implementations encounter parsing and semantic issues when handling IPv6 addresses in SIP messages, particularly around address formatting, port ambiguity, and differences between standards specifications.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides a collection of test messages organized by category: parser stress tests, valid and invalid messages with IPv6 references, port ambiguity cases, Via header variations, SDP integration, multiple IP addresses, IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses, and RFC 3261 ABNF edge cases.
tldr.outcome: Developers use these test cases to verify that their SIP implementations handle IPv6 correctly and robustly according to RFC 3261, following the Robustness Principle to accept variations while sending only strictly conformant messages.

today: RFC 5118 remains a standard reference for testing IPv6 support in SIP implementations. It has not been obsoleted. The RFC is frequently cited in implementation guidance and interoperability test plans. Developers implementing SIP on modern dual-stack networks rely on these test cases to verify correct behavior.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 5118 is a companion to RFC 4475 (the general SIP Torture Test document), focusing specifically on IPv6 network identifiers. It provides example SIP test messages designed to exercise and stress the code of IPv6-enabled SIP implementations. The document is informational and does not change SIP specifications; rather, it clarifies behavior through examples.

The RFC acknowledges that system-level issues like deploying dual-stack proxy servers, DNS configuration with both A and AAAA records, and media handling all play roles in IPv6 transition. However, those topics are addressed elsewhere; this document focuses solely on message parsing and semantic correctness for IPv6 addresses in SIP.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is a test suite. It shows what kinds of tricky messages SIP software might receive and makes sure the software can handle them without breaking.

sections.title: Test Message Organization
sections.content:
The RFC uses documentation IPv6 addresses from the 2001:DB8::/32 prefix (reserved by RFC 3489) and documentation IPv4 addresses from 192.0.2.0/24 (per RFC 3330). Many examples exceed the RFC's 72-character line limit, so the document uses an <allOneLine/> markup convention (from RFC 4475) to show how folded lines are reconstructed.

Some examples are valid SIP messages conforming to RFC 3261 grammar; others are intentionally invalid. The document clearly marks whether each message is well-formed and what makes invalid messages incorrect.
sections.plainLanguage: The test messages use fake addresses that are safe to show in examples. Some messages are correct, some are broken on purpose, to teach the software what to accept and reject.

sections.title: Parser Torture Tests
sections.content:
The RFC presents ten categories of test messages. The first covers valid SIP messages with IPv6 references in the Request-URI, Via header, and Contact header, all using the mandatory [ and ] delimiters. The second tests invalid messages (such as IPv6 addresses missing the delimiters), which should trigger a 400 Bad Request error.

Later tests stress port handling: one test shows a message where a port number appears ambiguous (5070 looks like the last octet of the IPv6 address because it is inside the closing bracket). Another shows unambiguous port notation with the port outside the closing bracket. Two tests stress the Via header's received parameter, which according to RFC 3261 should NOT have brackets around the IPv6 address, though robust implementations accept both forms.
sections.plainLanguage: The tests check if software can: handle IPv6 addresses with brackets, reject ones without brackets, figure out where a port number starts and stops, and accept both bracket styles in the Via received field.

sections.title: IPv6 in SDP and Multiple Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC includes tests for IPv6 addresses in the Session Description Protocol (SDP) body carried by SIP. Unlike SIP headers, IPv6 addresses in SDP do not use brackets. One test shows an INVITE with IPv6 addresses in both the SIP header and the SDP body, demonstrating the two syntaxes side by side.

Additional tests cover multiple IP addresses: one message contains multiple Via headers with both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses (and different protocols); another contains SDP with mixed IPv4 and IPv6 connection addresses on different media lines. A final test covers IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses (notation like ::ffff:192.0.2.1) appearing in signaling, SDP, and Contact headers.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP headers use brackets for IPv6 addresses, but SDP (the media description part) does not. A single message can have both styles, and software must handle each correctly in its own context.

sections.title: RFC 3261 ABNF Edge Cases
sections.content:
The RFC identifies a bug in RFC 3261's IPv6 reference ABNF, inherited from RFC 2373 (now obsoleted by RFC 4291). The ABNF allows an extra colon before the IPv4 part of an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address, producing constructs like [2001:db8:::192.0.2.1] (note the three colons). The correct form is [2001:db8::192.0.2.1] (two colons).

Following the Robustness Principle (RFC 1122), implementations should tolerate both forms when receiving messages but should send only the correct form. The RFC provides test cases for both the buggy and correct syntax, allowing implementations to demonstrate robust parsing.
sections.plainLanguage: The standard's grammar accidentally allows an extra colon in some IPv6 addresses. Strict reading of the rules allows the extra colon, but modern IPv6 rules forbid it. Smart software accepts both when reading but only sends the correct form.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that while it provides examples of SIP messages with IPv6 addresses, it does not change base SIP security considerations in RFC 3261. The document helps implementations handle edge cases and malicious input correctly.

The authors caution that parsers must carefully consider edge conditions and handle crafted input safely. Many attacks on Internet systems exploit parsing weaknesses by providing unusual inputs. While RFC 5118 does not attempt to catalog every possible attack, it covers common pitfalls discovered during IPv6 SIP implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: These test messages are like practice drills for security. They show some of the tricky inputs that could break bad software, and developers should make sure their code handles them safely.
